notes.meaning: The title shows this psalm was meant to be sung in public worship, led by the choir leader. In the Bible, a "fool" is not someone slow in mind but someone who turns away from God for moral reasons. He says "There is no God" in his heart, often because he wishes there were no God to judge him. He may never say it out loud, yet he lives as if God does not rule the world. Bible teachers call this being a "practical atheist." Leaving God out like this leads to corrupt and ugly living.

God knows all things already. Here He is pictured in human terms, leaning down from heaven to look closely at people. This recalls how He came down to see the tower of Babel and the evil before the Flood. He is searching for anyone who truly understands and seeks Him, and He would gladly find such a person. The test is about the heart, not about how clever someone is.

God's search finds no one who does good on their own. People have turned away from Him and have "gone sour," like spoiled milk. Paul quotes these verses in Romans 3 to show that everyone, Jew and non-Jew alike, is under the power of sin. Any good in a person is God's work through His grace, which changes the heart.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient Greek and Latin copies of the psalm add six more lines after this verse, the same ones Paul uses in Romans 3:13-18. Many scholars think these lines were copied into the psalm from Romans, though they were read in churches very early.

notes.meaning: God asks with surprise whether evildoers will ever learn. They may think God's people are the foolish ones, but they are the ones who truly lack understanding. They "devour" God's people as easily, greedily and often as eating a meal, with no guilt at all. They also never pray, because living without God always means living without prayer.

Just where the wicked felt strong and safe, sudden terror grips them. The Hebrew says "they feared a fear," a deep dread that comes when conscience strikes or God steps in. They are afraid because God stands with the righteous, and fighting His people means fighting Him.

David now speaks straight to the evildoers. They mock and block the plans of poor, troubled believers, and scorn them most of all for trusting God. But their efforts will fail, because the LORD is a safe hiding place for His people. Believers should not let anyone laugh them out of their trust in Him.

The psalm ends with a longing prayer that God's rescue would come from Zion, where God's presence was known among His people. "Captivity" here can mean any great trouble or oppression, not only exile. Many teachers also see a deeper hope: the coming of the Messiah, God's promised Savior, to deal with sin and set His people free. When God acts, all His people will rejoice.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think this verse, or even the whole psalm, comes from the time when Israel was in exile in Babylon. They read it as a prayer for the captives to return home.
